title: It’s Never Been Easier to Build, and Never Been Harder to Build Something That Holds

Product Management Artificial Intelligence Product Strategy Ai Product Management Product Development It’s Never Been Easier to Build, and Never Been Harder to Build Something That Holds Inbal Gilead 3 min read · Sep 22, 2026 -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size In fast-changing AI markets, teams can execute successfully against assumptions that are no longer true. Durable products come from making those assumptions visible and building ways to detect and handle change. Over the past year, I worked with Swimm on building an AI-powered platform for code understanding. During that time, models improved, development accelerated, and capabilities that seemed ambitious only months earlier became increasingly available. But the most interesting change wasn’t in the technology. The Problem Itself Kept Moving As people became more invested in AI, they learned what models could do, but also where they failed. Their expectations changed accordingly. This created an unusual product environment: we’re building while the definition of a good solution is still changing. At Swimm, we initially assumed customers needed the product to be 100% accurate. So naturally, much of the work focused on accuracy and coverage. But over time, something shifted. As generative AI became common, users developed a more practical understanding of what working with it looks like. They became willing to accept some inaccuracy (although exactly how much remains hard to estimate) in exchange for a faster, integrated output that allowed them to validate, build on it, and keep moving. The product’s value proposition changed; Instead of only asking, “How do we make every output perfect?” we also started asking: How do we help customers get dependable value from outputs that may not be perfect? I find that these days this is where many products get stuck: teams continue to execute against drifting assumptions. Faster development can sometimes make this worse. Building faster makes it harder to notice the drift. Making Assumptions Visible When the problem space keeps changing, I find durability requires a learning system. Products need to tolerate changes in model capabilities, customer expectations, and usage patterns without losing their core value. That starts with making assumptions visible: What do we believe customers need today? Which trade-offs are we making for them? What signals would tell us their priorities have changed? And what must remain true for the product to stay valuable? In the Swimm example, “100% accuracy” initially represented trust. But it wasn’t the only way to create it. Traceability- the ability to review and verify the output- could also make the product dependable. Understanding this helped us make better decisions about what to prioritize and what the product needed to own; this drove an entirely new product section that became our core differentiator against competition. There’s a meaningful lesson here for product leadership. As execution becomes easier, our job is increasingly to create the conditions for good judgment: make the team’s assumptions explicit, define the signals that could challenge them, and treat changes in customer behavior as product information. The products that hold won’t necessarily be the ones that keep up with every new capability or build faster than everyone else. They’ll be the ones that know which value they’re providing — and can quickly identify and handle the changes around it.
